passage: My name is Nikita. In Class Five I got a low mark in the maths test, and I put the paper at the bottom of my bag. The paper needed my mother Arohi's signature. Every evening I told myself, "Tomorrow." At dinner I talked very loudly about anything else. The paper felt heavier each day, like a stone I had to carry to school and home again. On the fifth day, my mother stopped stirring the dal and said, "You've been quiet in a strange way. Is something on your mind?" My voice shook. I took out the paper. She said, "Thank you for showing me. Let's look at it together," and I cried a little.

qa.q: Where did Nikita put the maths paper?
qa.a: At the bottom of the bag.

qa.q: What was Nikita feeling every evening while saying "Tomorrow"?
qa.a: Afraid and burdened. The paper felt heavier each day, like a stone Nikita had to carry.

qa.q: What made the first admission easier for Nikita?
qa.a: Arohi stopped stirring, asked calmly what was on Nikita's mind, and then said "Thank you for showing me. Let's look at it together."

qa.q: How might Arohi have felt watching Nikita talk loudly about anything else?
qa.a: Concerned and puzzled. Arohi noticed the strange quiet and gave Nikita a calm chance to say what was wrong.

grounding: Nikita avoids telling Arohi about a low grade, and the delay makes it heavier until Arohi's calm makes the first admission easier.

passage:
Note from Madhav, class teacher, parent-teacher day.
Rashmi's science mark dropped last month, and Rashmi had not shown the paper at home. In the corridor before the meeting, Rashmi kept looking at the door and twisting the bag strap. Rashmi's mother came in and I said we would talk together. Rashmi said in a small voice, "I got a very low mark. I was scared to tell." Rashmi's mother took a breath and said, "I'm glad you told me. Let's see what happened." She did not shout. Rashmi's shoulders dropped. I suggested a small plan: two short revision sessions a week with me, and I'll check in.

qa.q: What had Rashmi not shown at home?
qa.a: The science paper with the low mark.

qa.q: What was Rashmi feeling in the corridor, and what suggests it?
qa.a: Nervous and afraid of the reaction. Rashmi kept looking at the door and twisting the bag strap.

qa.q: What did Rashmi's mother do that made the admission easier?
qa.a: Rashmi's mother took a breath, said she was glad Rashmi told her, and asked what happened, without shouting.

qa.q: How might Madhav see the delay in telling?
qa.a: As common and understandable, since the fear of a reaction usually makes the talk harder than the news; Madhav offered support with a small plan.

grounding: A child avoids telling a parent about a low mark until it grows, and a calm parent makes the first admission easier.

passage: In their Osaka apartment, Yuki, ten, hid the maths test at the bottom of her school bag. Forty-two out of a hundred. Her classmate Leila had said, "Just don't show it. Parents forget." For a week Yuki didn't. Every evening she felt her stomach twist when her mother asked about school. Then the teacher sent a note home asking for a signature. Yuki had to sign it herself or tell. She sat at the kitchen table with the note, shaking. "Mama, I have to show you something. I've been hiding it." Her mother read it. She didn't shout. She sat down next to Yuki and said, "Thank you for telling me. I know that was hard. Let's look at what went wrong together." Yuki burst into tears, mostly from relief.

qa.q: What did Yuki score on the maths test?
qa.a: Forty-two out of a hundred.

qa.q: How did Yuki feel each evening while hiding the test?
qa.a: She felt anxious and guilty, her stomach twisting when her mother asked about school.

qa.q: What made the eventual talk easier for Yuki?
qa.a: Her mother stayed calm, thanked her for telling, and offered to look at the mistakes together.

qa.q: How might Leila's advice have made things worse?
qa.a: It encouraged Yuki to hide the test, so the worry grew for a week and the talk felt bigger.

grounding: Shows a child avoiding telling a parent about a low grade until it grows, and a calm parent making the admission easier.

passage: At the school counselling room, Sharmila, eleven, sat twisting her dupatta. Three weeks ago, she and Farida had a huge fight at lunch, and Sharmila had pushed Farida's tiffin off the table. Since then, they hadn't spoken, and Sharmila hadn't told Ammi. Every day, Ammi asked, "How's Farida?" and Sharmila said, "Fine." Today the class teacher had called Ammi in, because Farida's mother had complained. Sharmila's face was burning. She hadn't slept properly in days. When Ammi walked in, Sharmila couldn't look at her. But Ammi sat down, put a hand on her back and said, "Beta, I'm not angry. I just wish you'd told me three weeks ago. What happened?" Sharmila's words came tumbling out. By the end, she was crying. "I didn't know how to start." Ammi hugged her. "Next time, start with 'Ammi, something happened.'"

qa.q: What did Sharmila do to Farida's tiffin?
qa.a: She pushed it off the table.

qa.q: How did Sharmila feel before Ammi walked in?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and anxious, her face burning, not having slept properly in days.

qa.q: What did Ammi do that made it easier to talk?
qa.a: She stayed calm, said she wasn't angry, gently asked what happened, and offered a simple way to start next time.

qa.q: How might Farida have felt during the three weeks?
qa.a: She was probably hurt and upset, enough that her mother complained to the school.

grounding: Shows a child avoiding telling a parent about a quarrel until it grows, and a calm parent making the admission easier.

passage:
Monday: Kavitha got 6 out of 20 in the science quiz. She folded the paper into her geometry box and told Appa, "It went okay."
Wednesday: The next quiz was 8 out of 20. She hid that too. At dinner her brother Sumit asked, "Didn't you have a quiz?" Kavitha changed the subject.
The next Monday: The teacher's note came asking Appa to meet. Sumit found Kavitha crying on the stairs. "Tell him now," he said. "It'll be worse tomorrow." Kavitha went to Appa's room. "Appa, I've been hiding two quizzes." Appa read them, then pulled her close. "Two bad quizzes aren't the end of the world. Hiding them makes it heavier. Let's make a plan." Kavitha let out a breath she'd been holding for a week.

qa.q: What did Kavitha score on Monday's science quiz?
qa.a: 6 out of 20.

qa.q: How did Kavitha feel as the hiding went on?
qa.a: She felt more anxious and burdened, ending up crying on the stairs.

qa.q: What made the final talk easier?
qa.a: Sumit encouraged her to tell right away, and Appa responded calmly and offered to make a plan.

qa.q: How did Sumit see Kavitha's situation?
qa.a: He saw that waiting would only make it worse, and urged her to tell Appa now.

grounding: Shows a child hiding low grades until the problem grows, and a calm parent making the eventual talk easier.

passage: Urmila, you've been hovering near that report-card envelope all evening, so let me tell you about my Class 5. Your Nilesh Dada got 31 in arithmetic, in red ink. I hid the card inside my geography book. Every day I meant to tell my mother, and every day it felt heavier. I stopped eating my pakoras. I snapped at my brother. After two weeks the headmaster sent a boy to our house to ask why the card hadn't come back signed. Now there were two problems: the 31, and the hiding. My mother read the note, sat me down and said very quietly, "I'm not angry about the marks. I'm sad you carried this alone." I cried with relief. So, Urmila. Would you like to show me that envelope?

qa.q: Where did young Nilesh hide the report card?
qa.a: Nilesh hid it inside the geography book.

qa.q: How did young Nilesh feel during the two weeks of hiding?
qa.a: Young Nilesh felt guilty and weighed down, enough to stop eating pakoras and snap at a brother.

qa.q: What choice in the story made things worse, and what made them better?
qa.a: Hiding the card turned one problem into two; the mother's calm, quiet words made it easy to admit it.

qa.q: How might Nilesh's mother have felt reading the headmaster's note?
qa.a: She was probably sad and a little hurt that Nilesh had carried it alone, which is exactly what she said.

grounding: Shows a child delaying telling a parent about a low mark until it grows, and a calm parent making the admission easier.
